outOfScope: attributing private intention from form alone

claims.claim: Form has three dimensions—height, width, and depth—whereas shape has only height and width.
Three-dimensional forms can be encountered from more than one side, while two-dimensional works can create the illusion of form using visual cues.
Geometric forms include regular, named volumes; organic forms are commonly irregular, asymmetrical, or biomorphic.
Close formal analysis can examine form alongside line, shape, space, color, texture, and pattern, and should not replace contextual methods for questions beyond visual evidence.
Openings and surrounding space can be relevant to a viewer's encounter with a three-dimensional work.
Material surfaces and lighting affect what features of a form become visible, but do not by themselves establish symbolic meaning or intent.
